reason: Points out that encryption works as a control on one side and a weapon on the other. That moves ransomware, the item I hesitated over, away from Confidentiality and toward the property it actually destroys (Availability).

Gives a test based on the attacker's goal (seen / changed / unusable) and says to ignore side-effect damage. That resolves ransomware ('it changes the files' vs 'denies use') and exfiltrate-then-post.
Gives a clean before-the-act vs evidence-afterwards test for the two identity properties. That settles the tamper-evident audit log, my main hesitation, as Non-repudiation rather than Authentication.

Gives a usable test for whose interest is served (organisation vs data subject) that separates Privacy from the identity pair. It is weaker than hint 0 because the Privacy items were already fairly clear.

Machine / rule people follow / physical barrier is close to a gloss of the three bucket names. It adds little for anyone who knows the categories, and a background check is a process rather than a 'rule people follow', so the hint doesn't clearly settle that item.

The thought experiment where everyone stops following instructions is a real test. It cleanly separates Administrative (AUP, background checks, explicitly 'paperwork or not') from the controls that keep working on their own, though it doesn't separate Technical from Physical.

The 'would you owe this if nobody hired you?' test resolves exactly what I hesitated over: admitting you lack the qualifications and declining a conflict of interest go to III, while honesty in a sales pitch to a not-yet-client goes to II.

It explicitly dismisses honesty, the distractor that pulls the qualification and sales-pitch items toward II, and replaces it with a test based on which relationship the situation sits inside. 'An engagement you have taken on' correctly excludes the prospect.

'Order by input dependencies' is generic sequencing advice that fits any ordering task. It doesn't touch the only real point of hesitation, whether residual-risk sign-off comes before or after applying and verifying the control.

Separating deciding, doing and signing off, and saying sign-off needs what the work actually achieved, puts 'Document residual risk' after 'Apply and verify'. That is exactly the step a learner might misplace.

A three-question routine (binding? how specific: goal / named setting / steps? internal or external?) maps every item to a single layer. It handles the hardened-OS and named-owner items I hesitated over.

Warns directly against the two classic errors: treating 'must' as Standard (the named-owner item is Policy) and treating 'names exactly what to use' as Procedure (AES-256 and the hardened image are Standards).
